questiontext.text:
Q1 — P = D INVERSE TIMES A

Section 7.1 noted that P = D−1A = I − Lrw: the random-walk Laplacian is literally 'one minus one step of the walk'.

Write transition(n, edges) for an undirected graph, returning the row-stochastic matrix P with P[u][v] = 1/du if u–v is an edge. An isolated node gets an all-zero row. Then write stationary(n, edges) returning the theoretical stationary distribution du/2m.

edges = [(0,1),(1,2)]
stationary -> [0.25, 0.5, 0.25]

Hint. On an undirected graph the stationary distribution is just the degree — which is exactly why long walks are uninformative and short ones are not.

testcode.text: print(stationary(3, [(0, 1), (1, 2)]))
P = transition(4, [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 0)]) print([round(sum(r), 6) for r in P])
P = transition(2, []) print(P, stationary(2, []))

# one step from the stationary distribution returns it unchanged n, e = 4, [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 0), (0, 2)] P = transition(n, e) pi = stationary(n, e) nxt = [sum(pi[u] * P[u][v] for u in range(n)) for v in range(n)] print([round(x, 8) for x in nxt] == [round(x, 8) for x in pi])

questiontext.text:
Q2 — PAGERANK

Teleportation makes the modified transition matrix strictly positive, hence irreducible and aperiodic; Perron–Frobenius then gives a unique positive fixed point reached geometrically at rate α. Dangling nodes must be handled explicitly or all the probability leaks away.

Write pagerank(n, out_links, alpha, n_iter), where out_links[u] is the list of successors of u. Start from the uniform vector and perform exactly n_iter iterations, redistributing the mass of dangling nodes uniformly over all n nodes. Return the rank list.

n = 2, out_links = [[1], [0]], alpha = 0.85
->  [0.5, 0.5]  (by symmetry)

Hint. r'v = (1−α)/n + α(dangling mass)/n + α∑u→v ru/|out(u)|

testcode.text: print([round(x, 6) for x in pagerank(2, [[1], [0]], 0.85, 50)])
out = [[1, 2], [2], [0], [2]] print([round(x, 5) for x in pagerank(4, out, 0.85, 100)])
# probability must be conserved, even with a dangling node out = [[1], [], [0]] r = pagerank(3, out, 0.85, 100) print(round(sum(r), 8))
# alpha = 0 gives the uniform distribution out = [[1, 2], [2], [0]] print([round(x, 6) for x in pagerank(3, out, 0.0, 20)])
# a node everyone points to should rank highest out = [[3], [3], [3], [0]] r = pagerank(4, out, 0.85, 200) print(r.index(max(r)))

questiontext.text:
Q3 — THE (p, q) SEARCH BIAS

node2vec is a second-order walk: the next step depends on where you came from. q > 1 keeps the walk local (BFS-like, structural equivalence); q < 1 pushes it outward (DFS-like, homophily). This one parameter decides what 'similar' will mean.

Write node2vec_probs(adj, t, v, p, q) returning a dict mapping each neighbour x of v to its normalised transition probability, using the unnormalised weight 1/p if x == t, 1 if x is adjacent to t, and 1/q otherwise.

adj = {0:[1], 1:[0,2,3], 2:[1,3], 3:[1,2]}
node2vec_probs(adj, 0, 1, 1.0, 1.0)  ->  {0: 0.333, 2: 0.333, 3: 0.333}

Hint. adj is a dict node -> list of neighbours. Build the weights first, then divide by their sum.

Q4 — COMMON NEIGHBOURS, JACCARD, ADAMIC-ADAR

Liben-Nowell and Kleinberg's classical scores remain strong, training-free baselines. Adamic–Adar's insight is that a shared rare neighbour is far more informative than a shared hub — hence the 1/log d weighting.

Given adj (a dict node -> set of neighbours), write common_neighbors(adj, u, v), jaccard(adj, u, v) (0.0 if the union is empty) and adamic_adar(adj, u, v). In Adamic–Adar skip any shared neighbour of degree ≤ 1, whose log is 0 or negative.

adj = {0:{2,3}, 1:{2,3}, 2:{0,1}, 3:{0,1}}
common_neighbors(adj,0,1) -> 2     jaccard -> 1.0

Hint. Adamic–Adar = ∑z shared 1/log(dz), natural logarithm.

testcode.text: adj = {0: {2, 3}, 1: {2, 3}, 2: {0, 1}, 3: {0, 1}} print(common_neighbors(adj, 0, 1), jaccard(adj, 0, 1))
adj = {0: set(), 1: set()} print(common_neighbors(adj, 0, 1), jaccard(adj, 0, 1), adamic_adar(adj, 0, 1))
adj = {0: {2}, 1: {3}, 2: {0}, 3: {1}} print(common_neighbors(adj, 0, 1), jaccard(adj, 0, 1))
